articles.title: Caso Master: Fachin mantém prisão do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente do STF seguiu parecer da PGR e apontou risco à ordem pública e às investigações sobre fraudes financeiras bilionárias. Ex-banqueiro está detido desde março.
articles.summary: Presidente do STF seguiu parecer da PGR e apontou risco à ordem pública e às investigações sobre fraudes financeiras bilionárias. Ex-banqueiro está detido desde março.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), Edson Fachin , manteve nesta quinta-feira (19) a prisão do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, do Master, alvo da Operação Compliance Zero .

Ele está preso desde 4 de março. Atualmente, Vorcaro está no 19º Batalhão da Polícia Militar do Distrito Federal, conhecido como Papudinha.

Vorcaro já foi indiciado pela Polícia Federal como líder de organização criminosa no inquérito que apura fraudes na compra do Master pelo Banco de Brasília (BRB).

Fachin seguiu entendimento da Procuradoria-Geral da República, que não vê excesso de prazo na prisão e nem "antecipação de pena".

Na decisão desta quinta, Fachin afirmou que os fundamentos que motivaram a prisão continuam presentes .

Segundo o presidente do STF, a detenção se justifica “pelos elementos convincentes que apontam participação de Vorcaro como principal agente de comando, coordenação e decisão da organização criminosa investigada, na condição de gestor e controlador do Banco Master”.

O ministro destacou que os elementos reunidos indicam a suposta atuação do investigado na captação fraudulenta de recursos no mercado financeiro .

“Apontam, ainda, sua interlocução direta com servidores do Banco Central, com acesso a orientações estratégicas e a documentos institucionais", afirmou Fachin.

"Revelam, também, sua suposta vinculação ao coordenador do núcleo responsável pelas atividades de monitoramento e obtenção de informações de interesse da organização criminosa, além de indícios de que, em tese, teria determinado a prática de atos de intimidação contra concorrentes empresariais, ex-empregados e jornalistas, bem como obtido informações antecipadas sobre diligências investigativas”, acrescentou.

O presidente do STF concluiu dizendo que, “no caso, a prisão preventiva segue, portanto, adequada e indispensável à aplicação da lei penal, à manutenção da ordem pública e à conveniência da instrução criminal, devendo ser mantida”.

Fachin também decidiu manter a prisão do policial federal aposentado Marilson Roseno da Silva, apontado como “chefe da Turma”, grupo de intimidação ligado a Vorcaro .

PGR: quadro que justifica prisão não se alterou

Para o procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, o quadro que justificou a prisão não se alterou ao longo do tempo, sendo que não há justificativa para revogação da prisão ou substituição por medidas alternativas, como uso de tornozeleira.

Entre os argumentos para manter a prisão, a Procuradoria cita a gravidade dos crimes investigados, o papel atribuído a Vorcaro na organização criminosa, seu poder de influência e a necessidade de interromper a atuação do grupo.

A PGR também afirma que há valores ainda não recuperados e possíveis movimentações financeiras no exterior.

"A custódia cautelar de Daniel Vorcaro fundamenta-se no risco concreto à ordem pública, à instrução criminal e à aplicação da lei penal", afirmou a Procuradoria.

articles.title: White House national cyber director is leaving the administration
articles.summary: Sean Cairncross has played a key role in crafting AI policy for the Trump administration. His immediate replacement is Kirsten A. Davies.
articles.body: White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving the Trump administration, a White House official confirmed Thursday. Cairncross will be replaced by Kirsten A. Davies, who currently serves as the chief information officer at the Defense Department, a source close to the White House told NBC News. Davies will serve in an acting capacity, the source said. The position requires Senate confirmation. Axios was first to report the personnel changes. Cairncross has served as head of the Office of the National Cyber Director since August 2025. The office oversees all government cybersecurity policy and strategy. He has been directly involved with the White House’s deliberations over AI policy, including after Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick directed Anthropic to take down its two most powerful AI systems over the summer due to national security concerns. Cairncross is leaving his post after a series of tech outages affected both private companies and government agencies over the past week. Administration officials as well as Democratic members of Congress have said the outages do not appear to be the result of cyberattacks, though some have suggested AI may have played a role. The White House, when reached for comment Thursday night, did not provide details about the staffing changes. Cairncross’ previous White House roles include senior adviser to the White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term. During the 2016 election cycle, Cairncross was the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer. He worked for the RNC again during the 2024 cycle, serving as then-chief operating officer Chris LaCivita’s deputy. The source close to the White House said Davies will strengthen the president’s cybersecurity team, which includes Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser. Rubio welcomed Davies to her new position in a social media post. “Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity,” Rubio wrote on X.

articles.title: California State Bar opens investigation into former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia
articles.summary: The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into Katie Zacharia who faced scrutiny during her brief stint as White House press secretary for call...
articles.body:
The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into Katie Zacharia, who faced scrutiny during her brief stint as White House press secretary for calling herself a lawyer despite never passing a bar exam.

The probe, which was made public on Thursday, comes in response to a complaint submitted last month by the nonprofit watchdog Campaign for Accountability alleging that Zacharia may have violated California law by touting herself as lawyer.

While Zacharia, a Huntington Beach native, received a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011, she did not pass the bar exam in California or any other state. Yet, since at least early 2025 she has described herself as a lawyer on national television and in podcasts, including on "The Greg Kelly Show" and CNN, and has been identified on screen as a lawyer in at least 18 appearances on Fox News, according to the complaint.

"Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie. In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime," the organization's executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a news release last month.

The watchdog's complaint alleges Zacharia claimed to have served as "outside counsel" to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation, and previously listed herself on LinkedIn as full-time General Counsel of Fix California, a nonprofit.

A spokesperson for Zacharia denied that she had violated any laws in a text message to The Times, calling the accusations "baseless."

"This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar's time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing," the spokesperson said.

Under California state law a person presenting themselves as being entitled to practice law without an active state bar license could be charged with a misdemeanor and face up to a year in county jail and a $1,000 fine.

Zacharia addressed the scrutiny last month in an interview with conservative outlet Human Events, saying she had been preparing to take the bar exam in California shortly after getting married and was busy preparing for a move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing.

"I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I'd been long distance from for at least a year," Zacharia told the outlet, adding that the results of the exam were "somewhat inconsequential" because she knew she would not need the credential in China.

She said she had consulted several legal experts to ensure the title of lawyer was accurate when offering legal analysis and "they said absolutely, absolutely across the board. You can call yourself a lawyer," she told the outlet.

Zacharia added that it was "unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy."

Times staff writer Clara Harter contributed to this report.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Trump ousts cyber director after tech outages spark criticism
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White ‌House said on Thurs...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White ‌House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking ‌and national security systems.

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face ​mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.

The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal ‌is the administration's first major ⁠personnel move since the outages.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer ⁠Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.

"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition ​of anonymity.

Cairncross ​said in a statement on Thursday night it ​was the "honor of a lifetime ‌to serve" in Trump's administration.

The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.

The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were ‌separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical ​changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored ​attack.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri ​on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should ‌brief lawmakers on the outages so ​they can "share with ​the American people what's happening here."

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need ​to be confirmed by ‌the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in ​January.

(Reporting by Courtney Rozen and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by ​Caitlin Webber, John Mair and Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title: Trump’s National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross fired amid widespread tech outages
articles.summary: President Donald Trump backed the firing of National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross over cybersecurity credentials, with Kirsten A. Davies stepping in.
articles.body:
National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out after President Donald Trump backed his firing over concerns he lacked the cybersecurity credentials for the job, Fox News has confirmed.

Kirsten A. Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will step into the position in an acting capacity.

Davies, who was Senate-confirmed, will join Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, White House technology advisor Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the administration's national security and cyber leadership team.

An administration official separately told Fox News that Cairncross did not want to serve another two years in the role. Cairncross took office Aug. 4, 2025, after Senate confirmation, and the exact date of his departure remains unclear.

Senior administration officials welcomed Davies' appointment on X.

"Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America's cybersecurity," Rubio wrote.

Clayton praised her background, writing, "With nearly two decades of leadership experience in the technology space, Kirsten Davies will be a strong asset for the Trump administration in her new position with the Office of the National Cyber Director. It has been my pleasure to work closely with Kirsten on national security matters, and I look forward to now working with her to navigate an increasingly dynamic and fast-moving cyber landscape."

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth wrote, "The Department congratulates Kirsten Davies on her new role as the National Cyber Director. Throughout her tenure at DOW, she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape."

Davies thanked Trump, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Hegseth in her own post on X, calling the moment a critical juncture for U.S. technology.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future. Under President Trump's leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future," Davies wrote. "I am honored to continue to serve."

The leadership shakeup follows a nearly weeklong stretch of technical disruptions that hit air travel, major banks, Microsoft services, Apple, Marriott, the National Weather Service and internal systems at the National Security Agency.

A Nov. 13 Federal Aviation Administration outage triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight cancellations after contractor work on air traffic control wiring overloaded the system.

Administration officials have pushed back against speculation that hackers or foreign adversaries were behind the disruptions. Rubio said Tuesday that officials found "zero evidence" tying the incidents together or to malicious actors, while Clayton said the outages appeared linked to routine software patches and system upgrades rather than a coordinated cyberattack.

The Office of the National Cyber Director and Cairncross did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Senate passes sweeping bill simplifying permitting rules to build in America
articles.summary: The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday night to pass a sweeping bill to simplify and overhaul permitting rules for energy and infrastructure projects.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday night to pass a sweeping bill to simplify and overhaul permitting rules for energy and infrastructure projects. The bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, was crafted by an unusual coalition of Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va.; Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. The legislation would revise and speed up environmental reviews with tighter deadlines; accelerate electricity transmission; restrict the power of federal agencies to revoke existing permits; and reduce chokepoints for approving and completing projects. To conservatives, it’s about cutting government bureaucracy. “For far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty,” Capito said. For liberals, it’s an opportunity to make it easier to build long-sought projects, including clean energy, and address high costs. “Democrats are focused on lowering energy costs, reducing emissions, and stopping data centers’ free ride,” Whitehouse said. “Americans will start to get some relief quickly if this bill passes.” In an attempt to alleviate Americans’ concerns about data centers, the bill would require “new data centers of 20 megawatts or more to pay the full incremental cost of the infrastructure built to serve them,” according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. The legislation sparked opposition from some environmental groups and Native American tribal organizations, which objected to easing reviews and consultation rules that can be used to protect their interests. The bulk of the opposition in the Senate came from Democrats. Still, the willingness to simplify permitting rules represents a philosophical shift for the Democrats who endorsed it. Part of the reason is that liberal policy experts recognized that existing laws hinder their own goals. “This removes a lot of the obstacles that hamstrung [Joe] Biden’s climate investments,” said Adam Jentleson, a former Senate Democratic aide and founder of the research group Searchlight Institute. “A big part of the Inflation Reduction Act — a lot of the projects couldn’t break ground because of all the red tape.” The bill still needs approval from the House, where Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., expressed optimism that Congress will send a bill to President Donald Trump’s desk. “Well, we want to see a bill pass both chambers,” Scalise said when asked if the House will take up the Senate version of the legislation. “Obviously, the details matter. ... Hopefully, they pass a good bill back, and if not, we’ll work out those differences. But we want to get a bill to the president’s desk, and that’s still got a great chance to happen.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said the clearest path to making a law is for the House to take the Senate’s measure and pass it, noting that it has been through extensive debate. “It has been litigated now for months. Continues to be,” Thune told reporters. “Everything gets more complicated over here procedurally, and if it were to go over there and then come back over here, I can’t predict what happens. So hopefully there’ll be the critical mass there to move it. ... It’s been through the full monty when it comes to the legislating process.”

articles.title: DOJ looks to dismiss Alaska Senate lawsuit
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) is looking to dismiss its lawsuit that was focused on blocking the certification of Alaska’s Senate race if Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D) won, according to Thursday court filings. This case centered on the DOJ’s anger over the presence of a spoiler candidate who shared the same name as incumbent Sen.…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) is looking to dismiss its lawsuit that was focused on blocking the certification of Alaska’s Senate race if Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D) won, according to Thursday court filings.

This case centered on the DOJ’s anger over the presence of a spoiler candidate who shared the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). It was decided by U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason on Nov. 1 that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., the third-party candidate, could appear on November ballots after he advanced to Alaska’s four-candidate ranked-choice election.

DOJ attorneys argued in new court documents that the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals should overrule the previous dismissal of their case in order to effectively remove its loss but still urged the federal court to dismiss the case.

“This Court should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground,” the lawyers wrote.

“For Alaskans, there is only one direction: forward,” Peltola told The Hill in a statement. “Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I’m eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.”

The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projected Peltola’s victory over Dan Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and Republican Gerald Heikes on Wednesday.

The DOJ’s case was filed before the New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats were allegedly involved in an effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan. Federal probes into the matter were launched, though Peltola denied any knowledge of the plan.

President Trump demanded in October that Peltola be removed from the race and stated he believed Alaskan voters would get confused between either Dan Sullivan.

When the race was called by DDHQ, Peltola was still in the lead even if the votes for the senator and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. were combined, with 94 percent of the votes counted.

articles.title: Family of Robb Elementary victim hope their experience inspires mass casualty preparedness at hospitals
articles.summary: Javier choked up as he spoke about the moment he and his family identified the body of their nine-year-old daughter, Jackie. She was one of the 19 students who was shot and killed by an 18-year-old gunman at Robb Elementary in Uvalde.
articles.body:
ROUND ROCK, Texas (Nexstar) — Javier Cazares wiped away the tears streaming down his face.

His wife, Gloria, is seated next to him and hands him a couple of tissues. The duo just relived the darkest day of their lives for a room full of first responders from around the country.

Javier choked up as he spoke about the moment he and his family identified the body of their nine-year-old daughter, Jackie. She was one of the 19 students who was shot and killed by an 18-year-old gunman at Robb Elementary in Uvalde.

Javier said he lifted the sheet that covered his daughter’s body, curious to see what injury killed her. “She had one single shot. A bullet wound to the chest,” Javier said through tears.

“I played that last moment over and over in my head. Was she scared? What were her final thoughts,” Gloria said about her daughter’s last moments alive as she remained trapped in the classroom for more than a hour with the gunman, as more than 300 law enforcement officers stood outside.

The Cazareses were not in Round Rock to recount the failures of law enforcement that day. They were invited to the annual convention of the Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training (ALERRT) center. Their mission this week was to talk about their concerns with the medical care Jackie received after the gunman was killed, and why it is important that EMS, police, and fire collaborate with local hospitals to create procedures on what to do in a mass casualty event.

“What we’re trying to do is get people to understand and to learn the lesson, not just our police officers, but also the health care team that’s going to take care of our children after a traumatic event,” Gloria explained.

Javier said there was no communication from medical professionals at the hospital their daughter was taken to after the shooting. The family said they waited four hours before being asked to identify Jackie’s body.

Gloria said the chest seal used on Jackie’s body at the school was too large and did not fit properly. She added that the stretcher was too big for Jackie and that her daughter almost fell off it as she was being wheeled to an ambulance.

ALERRT is the gold standard of training law enforcement agencies across the country on active shooter events. But the center is pushing hospitals to have a plan in place for a possible mass casualty event, where a hospital can quickly become overwhelmed by multiple gun shot victims.

“Those hospitals that are prepared, those are going to be the ones where people are going to survive, and they’re not going to become overwhelmed,” James Keith, the director for external affairs at the ALERRT Center, said.

In 2025, former Uvalde Mayor Don McLaughlin passed a bill as a state representative in the 89th session to mandate ALERRT training for law enforcement agencies in Texas. ALERRT said it is not looking for a similar mandate for hospitals at this time, but it hopes the Cazares’ story will inspire action from hospital systems and law enforcement.

“Jackie wasn’t just another number,” Gloria said. “She was a little girl that had dreams and she should have had a bright future. And they talk a lot about the ‘why’ here, and hopefully Jackie can be somebody’s why.”

articles.title: Russell Brand’s crimes were an ‘open secret’: Why didn’t anyone stop him?
articles.summary: Why is the same industry that protected Brand and other men, like Harvey Weinstein, making projects about them?
articles.body:
Editor’s Note : This story contains discussions of rape or sexual assault that may be disturbing. Reader discretion is advised. If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, you can find help and discreet resources on the National Sexual Assault Hotline website or by calling 1-800-656-4673.

( NewsNation ) — Russell Brand seemingly once had it all until it came crashing down in the last few weeks after he was convicted of rape and sexual assault by a U.K. jury.

The conviction and sentencing — the comedian was given 10.5 years — may have been the first time the public even heard about the controversy surrounding him, but Brand’s behavior was apparently well-known in Hollywood .

Stakeholders also protected the actor, which begs the question: Why is the same industry that protected Brand and other men, like Harvey Weinstein, making projects about them?

Following his sentencing, Netflix released the documentary “ Russell Brand: Open Secret ,” which reflects on his past, but also discusses how his fellow comedians used to speak about the salacious and criminal things he was accused of doing.

Brand’s predatory persona was the act itself for all these years. It appeared in his stand-up, his radio show and his films, which makes me wonder whether the public found it harder to take the allegations against him seriously.

“It 100% helped him. I think that his public persona. He’s this sexual guy, he’s outrageous, he’s deliberately inappropriate, he’s so funny,” Los Angeles Magazine contributor Lauren Conlin told me.

She adds, “It just gave him this remarkable amount of cover. Some people would just say, ‘Oh, you know, that’s just that’s Russell being Russell.’”

The “Get Him to the Greek” actor took his sexual predation as a “joke,” says Conlin, who says Brand believed his fame protected him.

Daniel Sloth was the only comedian who would go on record about the allegations and how the accusations had been well-known in comedy for years.

Yet even after news broke about Brand, many people weren’t willing to speak up.

“I think it’s tough just because these industries are actually small,” said Conlin. “They hear these things thirdhand,” and may not speak about it because it isn’t something they’ve directly experienced.

“Some people also just want to mind their own business,” she said. “I am wondering who else is going to come out and be like, look, I should have said something.’’

articles.title: Army postpones controlled lead detonation after pleas from Iowa lawmakers
articles.summary: Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced he would be postponing Friday’s detonations of lead azide barrels in Iowa amid heavy pushback from lawmakers who say they were given short notice about the planned explosions. “Public safety is the Army’s top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow’s controlled detonation at the…
articles.body:
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced he would be postponing Friday’s detonations of lead azide barrels in Iowa amid heavy pushback from lawmakers who say they were given short notice about the planned explosions.

“Public safety is the Army’s top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23,” Telle wrote on social media .

He continued that delaying the explosion until Monday would be “the latest possible moment” before a forecasted temperature drop would further destabilize parts of the lead azide, which are typically used as explosives for secondary bombs.

The acting Army secretary said the lead azide was first discovered in March and started working immediately with “stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed.”

“In coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency, experts, and the local community, it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” he stated. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”

The Army announced the detonation in a Nov. 15 press release . Nearby residents were asked to vacate the area from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. local time on Friday before its delay.

“While safety measures will be fully enforced, the controlled detonation will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead,” the release said. “Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise; feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations; and will see a plume of dust.”

Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) expressed that “an unacceptable lack of communication and clarity” had made Iowans stressed about the situation.

Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa) stated that it was “ deeply troubling ” the Army didn’t give prior notice to outgoing Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) or other public officials. Outgoing Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) similarly remarked that she believed surrounding communities “were not given adequate notice.”

NEW YORK — Melania Trump is celebrating her docuseries debut, stepping out for a Hollywood-style premiere of “Melania: The Series.”

The first lady traded the White House for the black — rather than red — carpet on Thursday night, as she marked the forthcoming release of her two-part Prime Video series.

“You will see my beliefs, my principles, what I think about family trust, also pride and honor,” Trump told reporters.

Despite being in the spotlight for years, Trump told ITK in an interview that some of the public still has misconceptions about her.

“People they don’t really want to know, maybe, or they don’t focus on what I do,” Trump said. “They prefer to gossip, and they go in [a] different direction. And if they see what I do, I think it would be much more important.”

The series, to be released on Friday, has been touted by Prime Video as a project that offers audiences “an intimate look” at the 56-year-old author and former model as she navigates stepping into the role of first lady again in 2025 following President Trump’s second inauguration. The first episode is focused on family and trust, while the second part of the series, titled “Pride and Honor,” explores “the immediate responsibilities of serving as first lady.”

The release of the docuseries comes nearly a year after Trump made her documentary film debut. “Melania,” which reportedly cost Amazon MGM Studios $75 million, followed the first lady in the days before the 2025 presidential inauguration. The film reportedly grossed more than $16 million after it was released in January.

Amid the President Trump’s low approval rating and the GOP’s crushing losses in the midterm elections, it’s unclear if there’s an appetite for more first lady-focused fare.

But Marc Beckman, Melania Trump’s exclusive senior adviser, said that now was the right time for the first lady to share her story.

“I think it was a result of, for years and years, people asking her to see more, to understand more, and this is the truth,” Beckman said. “So you see a person that’s hardworking, committed to her family, committed to foster care children and children all over the world, and she opens this up to the world.”

The premiere at New York’s Lincoln Center drew a gathering of figures from all avenues of Trump’s life: “Melania” director Brett Ratner, fashion designer Hervé Pierre — who helped craft her inaugural gowns — and former Attorney General Pam Bondi, among others, all on-hand for the event. President Trump, who traveled back to the U.S. on Thursday following summits as well as bilateral and trilateral meetings in Asia, did not attend the event.

While her series will soon premiere on Prime Video, Trump said she doesn’t binge watch any shows herself.

“I don’t have time. I’m reading some executive orders actually, so maybe we pass some more,” she said, noting her work on women’s health and her Fostering the Future initiative.

“My time here is now. I want to focus here now, and let’s see what the future brings,” she said.

When asked by ITK if she’ll miss Washington when the president leaves office, Trump — who splits her time between the nation’s capital, Palm Beach, Fla., and New York — replied, “We love D.C. We love the White House. It’s a beautiful place.”

And what might the post-White House future hold for Trump?

“It’s too early to say,” she said with a smile.

articles.title: Pro-life group says Trump admin didn't give key abortion drug commitments before Overton FDA nomination pulled
articles.summary: Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America opposed Heidi Overton's FDA confirmation until the Trump administration committed to ending mail-order abortion drugs.
articles.body: A leading pro-life group said it opposed advancing Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration without commitments from the Trump administration on abortion drug policy. The White House withdrew her nomination this week amid questions about her support in the Senate. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said his group asked the Senate to hold up Overton’s confirmation until it received "firm commitments" from the administration on two fronts regarding abortion drug policy. Baptist said the group wants the next FDA nominee to commit to ending mail-order access to abortion drugs authorized under the Biden administration and changing how the agency studies the safety of those pills. "Right now, we’re seeing more abortions in this country than before the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade," Baptist said. "That’s precisely because of what the Biden FDA did to authorize mail-order abortion drugs. We’re seeing upwards of 15,000 abortion drugs and abortions occurring in pro-life states. Those states can’t meaningfully enforce their laws while this nationwide policy is in place." WHITE HOUSE PULLS TRUMP'S FDA PICK HEIDI OVERTON ON EVE OF SENATE PANEL VOTE "Under the Biden-era policy, anybody can obtain these drugs online and receive them through the mail," he continued. "When I say anybody, we’ve seen news story after news story every week about men and other predators obtaining these drugs to coerce or poison women into taking them against their will. Until that policy changes, no pregnant woman is safe from these drugs. My question to this administration is: How many more women have to be poisoned or coerced with abortion drugs before you take action on this drug?" Under the Biden administration, the FDA eliminated the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, allowing it to be prescribed without an in-person visit by certified prescribers and dispensed by certified pharmacies through the mail. On the group's second point of concern, Baptist said the FDA needs to conduct a new study to show the safety — or lack thereof — of mifepristone. "The problem is that the study is significantly flawed," he said. "It’s almost designed to fail and not lead to future changes to the drug regimen. We have asked for more robust data because significant information is currently lacking, including transparency into the agency’s methodology and an invitation for outside experts who have studied this drug over the last few decades." "This is something that should be bipartisan. Everybody should support better data, more transparency and outside experts who can inform an agency that has never conducted such a study before," he added. Several pro-life groups and Republican lawmakers have urged the Trump administration to complete the FDA’s safety review of mifepristone and consider reinstating safeguards, while some have called for removing the drug from the market. The FDA said the review is ongoing, with study results expected in December 2026 and a final report expected by March 2027. The White House pulled Overton’s nomination to lead the FDA earlier this week, one day before a Senate committee vote. President Donald Trump picked Overton, a physician and White House advisor, in August to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned from the position in May. Kyle Diamantas has led the agency in an acting capacity since Makary’s departure. WOMAN WHO SAYS ABORTION PILLS NEARLY KILLED HER URGES RFK JR TO ACT AS GROUP DEMANDS MAIL-ORDER CRACKDOWN Overton also previously served as vice chair and chief policy officer at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank, where she criticized expanded access to abortion pills in a 2023 policy brief. The White House said Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination, although Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, contended that he believed she could have been confirmed. "The White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members," Cassidy, R-La., wrote on X. "I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate." Baptist said he did not know whether the White House was concerned about pro-life votes or other constituencies but thinks Cassidy "was making progress with the administration to secure the commitments we were seeking and asking the Senate to hold the administration accountable for." Cassidy had criticized Overton for supporting Trump’s decision to recommend changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, but the senator said he had been convinced she was right for the job after she committed to "follow the science." She had appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office as the president signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including a recommendation to administer measles, mumps and rubella vaccines separately once individual shots become available domestically. Cassidy said at a September hearing that there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination. "Yes, senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy. Pressed on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., questioned why she had not corrected Trump in the Oval Office. "Why should we expect you to stand up to the president as FDA commissioner?" Markey asked. Baptist said he wants the next FDA commissioner to be somebody who "understands science" and has experience managing an agency. "The FDA is a very large bureaucracy with multiple constituencies, so understanding how science is conducted and how drugs are approved will be essential to any successful candidate or nominee for the position," he said. But, Baptist said, the administration does not have to wait for an FDA nominee to take the position before it can take the action on abortion pill policy that his group desires. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The good news is that it doesn’t have to be the nominee who makes these commitments. The administration can do it because it has admitted that it can take these actions immediately using its own authority," he argued. "That power is within the administration’s possession. It’s a matter of political will, not legal ability." "With regard to fixing the study, I think they can make those changes now," Baptist continued. "They don’t need to wait for a confirmation, especially when they’re saying they’re going to finish the study in December of this year. We might not have an FDA commissioner at that point, or even a nominee. So they need to fix it immediately and course-correct the study before it’s fatally flawed and completed next year." Fox News' Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

articles.title: Pedro Sánchez, sobre inmigración: "No hay pruebas de que Marruecos esté detrás de la crisis migratoria de Ceuta"
articles.standfirst: El candidato socialista defiende en el debate las vías legales y un plan de integración
articles.summary: El candidato socialista defiende en el debate las vías legales y un plan de integración
articles.body: El choque llega en un momento de máxima igualdad demoscópica y servirá de antesala al debate a cuatro previsto para el próximo jueves 26. Durante dos horas, el presidente del Gobierno y el líder de la oposición buscarán decantar a un electorado aún volátil en una cita que puede marcar el destino de la próxima legislatura. La gestión migratoria protagonizó el último bloque del debate cara a cara a diez días de las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. En un país que alcanzó en octubre los 10,43 millones de residentes nacidos en el extranjero —tras contabilizar 6,55 millones de llegadas y 3,35 millones de salidas entre 2018 y 2024, además de 1,43 millones de nacionalizaciones hasta 2025—, el presidente del Gobierno defendió la necesidad de atraer mano de obra foránea. Frente a las críticas del líder popular, el candidato socialista sentenció: "Necesitamos el aporte de la inmigración el Estado de Bienestar español". Para respaldar este modelo en la próxima legislatura, Sánchez trasladó al debate los compromisos económicos y laborales recogidos en el programa electoral del PSOE. El eje central pasa por desplegar el Plan de Integración y Ciudadanía 2026-2030, dotado con 500 millones de euros iniciales, más de 100.000 plazas de Formación Profesional y aprendizaje de lenguas oficiales, bajo la premisa programática de que "la integración es un compromiso de doble sentido, con derechos y obligaciones para todos". Asimismo, su hoja de ruta plantea agilizar la homologación de títulos, simplificar trámites y contratar en origen para aprovechar "el talento de quienes vienen a vivir y trabajar aquí". La dimensión exterior y el control fronterizo marcaron el intercambio más tenso entre ambos aspirantes. Ante los reproches de Feijóo sobre la crisis migratoria de Ceuta y la relación con Rabat, Sánchez replicó defendiendo la diplomacia preventiva frente a las acusaciones sin sustento: "No hay pruebas de que el gobierno de Marruecos esté detrás de la crisis migratoria de Ceuta". En esa misma intervención, el jefe del Ejecutivo reivindicó la colaboración transfronteriza contra las mafias y subrayó: "Necesitamos articular políticas de buena vecindad con nuestros vecinos, se llama Francia, Portugal o Marruecos". El presidente vinculó también su estrategia migratoria al marco comunitario y al rechazo a los postulados más restrictivos del espectro político. Tras cuestionar directamente a su rival preguntando "¿Qué ha traído bueno la ultraderecha al mundo?", Sánchez sacó pecho por los acuerdos alcanzados en Bruselas para gestionar los flujos de manera coordinada: "Hemos logrado con la Unión Europea un gran pacto de inmigración en nuestro país que vamos a desarrollar". De forma paralela, su candidatura propone reforzar la acogida de menores no acompañados, ampliar visados humanitarios e impulsar un pacto de Estado contra los delitos de odio. Pese a detallar estas iniciativas de acogida e inserción laboral, la propuesta socialista evita fijar cupos máximos de entrada o endurecer los mecanismos de expulsión para quienes permanecen en situación irregular. Después de haber ejecutado una regularización extraordinaria durante 2026, el programa con el que Sánchez concurre a las urnas tampoco contempla nuevas regularizaciones masivas ni cambios en los criterios de arraigo o nacionalidad, centrando toda su apuesta en la ampliación de los cauces legales y la integración social.

articles.title: El 'otro' debate con las reacciones al traje de Pedro Sánchez: "Qué color es ese"
articles.standfirst: El color marrón empleado que ha provocado que se viralice y que siempre tiene un trasfondo con su elección
articles.summary: El color marrón empleado que ha provocado que se viralice y que siempre tiene un trasfondo con su elección
articles.body: Uno de los asuntos que más debates ha despertado ha sido el traje que llevó el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez. Repitió tono como hace pocos días hizo en la entrevista con Carlos Franganillo en Telecinco. El político socialista elegía un traje de color marrón topo compuesto de una corbata granate o burdeos, camisa blanca y zapatos marrones y responde a recomendaciones técnicas sobre la escenografía del plató y a la búsqueda de un tono neutro en pantalla. Pero ha llamado mucho la atención. A Sánchez le aconsejaron descartar el color gris precisamente por la gama cromática del plató según informó la periodista Esther Redondo en La Sexta. Pero hubo reacciones en todos los lugares al respecto de esa puesta en escena. De hecho, se ha debatido mucho sobre el tono... Es decir, un traje marrón que recuerda a la estética socialista de los años 80. Porque dicha elección llevaba de forma casi directa a la moda de aquella década, marcada por los cortes clásicos, los colores tierra y las prendas de pana. "Pedro Sánchez ha elegido como color d traje el mismo q cuando coges todos los colores de la plastilina y los mezclas? Ese mismo tono marrón/gris", "Si pierde Sánchez sin duda será culpa del color espantoso de su traje", "El color del traje de Pedro Sánchez lo saqué yo en la boda de mi Tío Pedro mezclando una Mirinda ,un coca cola ,un Seven Up un poco de ponche caballero , licor 43 y dos canapés de ensaladilla", "Pero Sánchez!!! Ya gana te Feijóo, y sin empezar el debate . ¿Quién coño se pone un traje marrón por la noche?", fueron algunas de las reacciones que generaron la puesta en escena del presidente del Gobierno. Causó impacto el tono.

articles.title: El vídeo de 11 segundos con el que el PSOE contesta a Feijóo tras el cara a cara: “Ya sabéis que yo no miento”
articles.standfirst: Los socialistas contraponen sus palabras con un gráfico de verificación
articles.summary: Los socialistas contraponen sus palabras con un gráfico de verificación
articles.body: El PSOE ha recuperado una declaración de Alberto Nuñez Feijóo para cuestionar su credibilidad en plena campaña electoral. La mañana después del debate cara a cara entre el presidente del Gobierno Pedro Sánchez y el candidato del Partido Popular, el partido socialista ha publicado un vídeo en la cuenta de ‘X’, en el que contrapone imágenes del líder popular anoche en la sede de los populares con un gráfico que compara comprobaciones suyas y del Presidente, acompañado del hashtag “FeijóoMentiroso”. “Ya sabéis que yo no miento”. Feijóo pronunció esta frase anoche justo después del cara a cara en Génova ante militantes del partido. En el debate de este jueves 19 ambos confrontaron sus propuestas para las elecciones del 29 de noviembre y protagonizaron un intercambio de acusaciones sobre la veracidad de sus respectivas afirmaciones. El montaje de 11 segundos primero muestra al dirigente rodeado de simpatizantes y después introduce una tabla con distintas categorías de verificación. La publicación utiliza esa sucesión de imágenes para presentar una contradicción entre su promesa y las conclusiones recogidas en el gráfico. La imagen difundida atribuye a Feijóo quince momentos comprobados: dos calificados como ciertos, seis como verdades a medias, seis como falsos y uno como no comprobable. Pedro Sánchez recoge diecisiete: diez ciertos, seis a medias y uno no comprobable. La publicación llega en un contexto de acusaciones cruzadas sobre la veracidad de los mensajes políticos. Durante el debate cara a cara, la comprobación de datos estuvo presente en la disputa entre los candidatos mientras diversos medios analizaban sus declaraciones. Óscar Puente hace una semana también criticaba a Feijóo y a los verificadores tras la entrevista con Jordi Wild en ‘The Wild Project’, donde se le acusaba especialmente de haber mentido en la fecha de la foto con Marcial Dorado.

articles.title: White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
articles.summary: CBS is reporting he has been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
articles.body:
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a string of tech outages which hit the National Security Agency (NSA), the US air traffic control system and some banks.

Sean Cairncross had been national cyber director since August 2025.

CBS, the BBC's US news partner, reported he had been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.

The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross was fired, in a move supported by President Donald Trump.

The news, first reported by Axios , follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.

Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".

But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.

Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?

Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.

In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.

He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.

The White House has not publicly confirmed the departure or given a reason to why Cairncross left his role.

articles.title: Trump will face reporters after historic Xi-Putin talks as war questions linger
articles.summary: President Donald Trump faces reporters Friday after Shenzhen summit with Xi Jinping and Putin yielded a nuclear risk pledge but no Ukraine breakthrough.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is set to face reporters Friday after wrapping up a historic visit to China that brought him together with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for unprecedented three-way talks. The leaders struck a warm diplomatic tone despite lingering questions over the war in Ukraine, nuclear arms negotiations and tensions in the Middle East — as well as stalled trade negotiations between the U.S. and China. The summit in Shenzhen marked the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, bringing Trump face-to-face with two of America's chief geopolitical adversaries. Washington has spent years arming Ukraine in its war against Russia, while the Pentagon has long identified China as its primary "pacing challenge" in the Indo-Pacific. Trump's scheduled press conference at noon on Friday will offer an opportunity to elaborate on what the meetings accomplished and whether the diplomatic discussions will lead to concrete agreements. CHINA BLOCKS BLOOMBERG REPORTER FROM TRUMP-PUTIN-XI MEETING OVER QUESTION TO TRUMP The gathering between the three world powers produced a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, maintaining stable energy supplies and reforming the United Nations, but stopped short of announcing major breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran. President Trump described his trip as "Great and Highly Consequential" in a Truth Social post announcing that he will hold a press conference at the White House midday on Friday. Trump last appeared in the briefing room on Nov. 9, 2026, with UFC CEO Dana White after the president joked about offering him the press secretary job. On Nov. 13, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a White House briefing regarding the FAA nationwide ground stop. The president has not had a press secretary since Katie Zacharia's few-day stint last month in the role succeeding Karoline Leavitt. Zacharia held one briefing on Oct. 13, 2026, but was removed from the job after widespread backlash regarding her ability to serve in the role and her claims to be an attorney. Throughout the China visit, Trump emphasized his personal relationships with Xi and Putin, praising the Chinese leader for an elaborate welcome that included a military flyover and referring to both presidents as friends. "President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship," Trump said during their bilateral meeting Thursday. "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it." Trump also told Xi that their friendship had grown closer over the years and predicted the two countries would avoid major problems as long as they remained in power. During a separate meeting with Putin, Trump greeted the Russian leader by calling him "my friend," despite the lack of a breakthrough in his longstanding efforts to negotiate an end to Russia's war in Ukraine. The president later expressed optimism about those efforts, saying he had spent much of his bilateral meeting with Putin discussing the conflict. "I think things are happening," Trump said during the trilateral meeting. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war." Putin also acknowledged that Ukraine had been a focus of his separate discussions with Xi and Trump, but the three leaders' joint declaration made no mention of the conflict or any new peace initiative. The summit also put nuclear arms control back in the spotlight months after the expiration of New START, the last remaining treaty limiting U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals. Trump argued that the three countries were uniquely positioned to reduce the world's nuclear stockpiles, while acknowledging the difficulty of persuading nuclear powers to give up their weapons. "Once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them," Trump said. TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL The leaders ultimately agreed to pursue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, but announced no binding arms reductions or timetable for negotiations. Trump also pointed to potential cooperation with China on Iran, asserting that Washington and Beijing shared an interest in preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon and keeping energy flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. "Both the United States and China have an interest in ensuring that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon," Trump said during his meeting with Xi. "We both feel that very strongly on both points," he added. The remarks were notable given China's economic ties to Tehran, including its purchases of Iranian oil, which have provided an important source of revenue for the Iranian government despite Western sanctions. Beijing's commercial relationship with Iran has complicated U.S. efforts to isolate Tehran, although Trump's remarks did not establish whether China had agreed to change its oil purchases or take additional steps to pressure Iran over its nuclear program. Trade was another focus of Trump's meeting with Xi, with the president touting what he described as progress toward a more balanced economic relationship and signaling that he would seek additional purchases of American agricultural products. Under what Trump called the "30-for-30" deal, he said the two countries had agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion in trade. "Our farmers have done very well, and I'll be asking you to do some more for our farmers," Trump said, adding that China had an "insatiable appetite" for American products. The discussions came as Washington and Beijing continued to navigate disagreements over tariffs, rare earth minerals and access to advanced technology. Trump also used the APEC summit to declare the United States the world leader in "superintelligence," making the assertion in Shenzhen, one of China's major technology hubs, as the two countries compete for dominance in artificial intelligence. But the most consequential diplomatic development remained the historic trilateral meeting, which Trump described as an opportunity for the three powers to pursue cooperation despite their disagreements. "We are really making history," Trump said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The president's Friday press conference is expected to provide further insight into whether the summit's pledges will translate into negotiations on nuclear weapons, additional trade commitments or progress toward ending the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Gen Z helped Democrats win. Now it may want new leadership
articles.summary: Gen Z delivered a decisive win for Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections. Now they may want to see change in party leadership. Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, is facing achallenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to become majority leader in the Democratic-controlled 120th Congress. Van Hollen is…
articles.body:
Gen Z delivered a decisive win for Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections. Now they may want to see change in party leadership.

Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, is facing a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to become majority leader in the Democratic-controlled 120th Congress.

Van Hollen is the progressive in the race, and is getting support from the left, including from Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.).

Gen Z activists The Hill spoke with particularly emphasized a desire for change. They see the leadership race as an opportunity to get fresh blood atop the party.

Peter McKenzie, a 26-year-old member of the progressive veteran group Common Defense, said people believe “a new majority needs a new approach.”

Dakota Hall, executive director of Alliance for Youth Action (AYA), voiced similar thoughts.

“People across the board want big, not small, change right now,” he said. “Democrats won these voters because they had the change vehicle on the ballot a couple weeks ago, and if they stop being that, these voters will leave.”

He said he can see this in Gen Z’s view of Schumer.

“They’re most skeptical about Chuck due to his ties to the establishment. This election was a turning of the page of this country, where young people want to see a whole crop of new leaders,” he added.

Schumer has been a longtime supporter of Israel, who opposed the Obama-era Iran nuclear deal. He’s become a critic of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, but Van Hollen has him on Israel, for accepting money from PACs, and for opposing progressive candidates El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan in primary battles. El-Sayed won his primary and the general election, as did Flanagan in Minnesota. Both are now supporting Van Hollen.

Gen Z is also less likely to support Israel, Gallup data shows , making this Van Hollen point stick out for younger people. Although Van Hollen ran as a pro-Israel Democrat as recently as 2016, he has evolved into a harsh critic of the country’s government since the Gaza war.

A willingness to change is another way to draw Gen Z in. Alex Edgar, founder of AWE Strategies, a consulting firm focused on engaging young people, did not say who he supports for majority leader, but he did say these elections are a way to show young Americans that the party is willing to change.

“Regardless of who becomes Senate majority leader, you can count on the fact that young people are going to pay attention to the types of policies that are prioritized in the coming years,” he said. “We are looking for leaders who are willing to take a stand and work to create an American dream again for young people.”

Polling doesn’t definitively show who Gen Z would prefer to lead the Senate majority.

A post-Election Day poll from The Economist/YouGov found that Generation Z has a more favorable view of Van Hollen than older Americans. Twenty-eight percent of respondents aged 18-29 held a favorable opinion of Van Hollen, compared to 18 percent of those aged 30-44, 14 percent of those 45-64 and 19 percent of respondents 65 and older.

Meanwhile, 24 percent of respondents 18-29 said they held a favorable opinion of Schumer, while 33 percent said they held an unfavorable opinion of the long-time New York senator.

Given the role Gen Z voters played in the Democratic midterm wins two weeks ago, perhaps the surprising thing about the polling is that Schumer is doing better with young Americans polled than older Americans.

More than 50 percent of Millennials, Gen Xers and Boomers reported holding an unfavorable opinion of Schumer.

Van Hollen also faces some challenges, as he’s less known than Schumer, a veteran politician who was lampooned on “Saturday Night Live” after the midterm elections.

Fifty-four percent of those in Generation Z said they “don’t know” how he would lead the Senate.

In March 2025, youth political organizations called out Schumer in a letter, titled “Gen Z to Schumer: Fight for Us or Step Aside,” for his leadership as Senate minority leader, saying it was “failing to meet the moment.”

The letter was signed by organizations including the Sunrise Movement, College Democrats of America, Gen Z Against Trump, United We Dream Action and Voters of Tomorrow after Schumer voted to pass a GOP-backed funding bill.

Members of Gen Z, notably, aren’t eligible to serve in the Senate yet, but that doesn’t mean they don’t pay attention to Senate politics.

The Economist/YouGov poll found that adults 18-29 are more likely to view Congress as the most powerful branch of government, and they have more faith in the institution than other generations.

While attitudes toward Congress’s effectiveness are low across the board, 12 percent of Gen Z respondents expressed a “great deal of confidence” in the legislative branch, compared to 6 percent of Millennials, 4 percent of Gen X and 3 percent of Boomers.

“This is striking such a nerve right now because the election was all about the status quo and the ways in which our current government has been failing so many Americans,” Edgar said. “The Republican and Democratic Parties are both in a position in which they have to earn the votes of their constituents.”

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

articles.title: House Republicans race for key roles in the fight over Democrat-led Trump probes
articles.summary: Republicans are jockeying for the top spot on pivotal committees that will serve as the Democratic Party’s biggest line of attack on the Trump administration after the departure of seasoned GOP leaders. The powerful House Oversight and Judiciary committees now have empty seats for ranking members, with Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) departing Judiciary to serve…
articles.body:
Republicans are jockeying for the top spot on pivotal committees that will serve as the Democratic Party’s biggest line of attack on the Trump administration after the departure of seasoned GOP leaders.

The powerful House Oversight and Judiciary committees now have empty seats for ranking members, with Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) departing Judiciary to serve as House minority leader, while Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) gave up the Oversight gavel in his bid for governor.

Whoever clinches the gavel will be front and center for a number of coming fights on Capitol Hill, as Democrats have vowed the next Congress will not only mean investigations of President Trump but also a review of how his policies are impacting the American public.

The openings have sparked the interest of both longtime panel members as well as those much further in seniority from the dais.

On Oversight, Rep. Pat Fallon (R-Texas) flagged his interest as far back as April, while Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas), a first-term lawmaker, has also said he plans to run to lead the House’s top investigative committee.

On Judiciary, Reps. Scott Fitzgerald (R-Wis.) and Laurel Lee (R-Fla.) have sent “Dear Colleague” letters announcing their intentions to run for the post.

“Now that we know that we’ll be going into the minority, I believe there will be a focus in the committee on investigations and possibly impeachments,” Lee said in a sit-down with The Hill.

“For me, I am a former judge in Florida, and so I bring the perspective of someone who is accustomed to understanding and talking about the law, explaining the law, and applying it,” she continued. “I believe that’s going to be very important as we go into this time in history, because that will be an essential element of the job of ranking member, to be able to discuss what is appropriate, what is inappropriate, and what does the law tell us governs our behavior.”

The race would pit Lee, a former prosecutor and manager in the impeachment of former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, against Fitzgerald, a former majority leader in the Wisconsin state Senate.

Fitzgerald said he is ready to go toe-to-toe with Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), a former constitutional law professor set to chair the panel.

“We’re talking to people about how we think we can fight back. I mean, I’ve been around Congressman Raskin enough to, I think, have a familiar idea of how he kind of approaches things, and so I think that could be really helpful in whoever the ranker is,” Fitzgerald said.

“We’re going to hold [Democrats’] feet to the fire on the promises they made during the election cycle. I mean, that’s first and foremost, right? I mean, if you’re going to talk about going after either the private sector or people in the administration or President Trump himself — I guess you’re going to work on affordability when you have a chance or when there’s an opportune time? How are they gonna do this?” he said, adding that he’s prepared to “talk about why we think some of this stuff is just a waste of time.”

The Judiciary landscape will also be quite different this year. In addition to Jordan’s ascension to leadership, many of the other long-term Republican members are departing the panel. Reps. Andy Biggs (Ariz.) and Tom Tiffany (Wis.) lost their bids for governor in their respective states while Rep. Chip Roy (Texas) was unsuccessful in his run for Texas attorney general and Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) was ousted in a primary after Trump backed his challenger.

Those moves and losses wipe out nearly every lawmaker more senior to Fitzgerald on the panel.

“The dais when I looked to my left, it was kind of shocking, but we had so many people either run for higher office, lost their primaries or just decided to retire. So very unusual in six years to be in that position,” Fitzgerald said, but he thinks he’s ready.

“It’s my leadership skills. I’ve been an Army officer, I’ve been the majority leader in the Wisconsin Senate. Now I think I’ve, within six years, ascended pretty quickly, and that’s because of my leadership skills, more than a law degree.”

Lee noted the panel needs to be prepared to take on a number of other issues, adding that immigration will be a hot button issue along with renewal of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), which allows the government to spy on foreigners located abroad.

“We also still have a very robust set of policy issues that exist within the Judiciary Committee, everything from intellectual property to FISA,” she said, noting that she was the sponsor of the 2024 bill that enacted 56 new reforms.

“The role of the ranking member, I believe, is to fight against aggressive, overreaching efforts by the majority, but also to ensure that where we can, we are working across the aisle to pass good legislation for the American people,” Lee said, adding that she’s had five bills passed and signed into law.

On Oversight, GOP members are also pushing to be at the forefront of combatting far-reaching Democratic investigations.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), expected to be Oversight chair next year, fired off a dozen letters on Wednesday demanding a series of targets linked to Trump preserve their documents and communications. Recipients included the president’s family members, allies, those with insight into the probe of deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her former adviser Corey Lewandowski.

Fallon wouldn’t spill the “secret sauce” he’s prepping for the GOP steering committee, which could select the new ranking members as early as December, but said responding to those investigations is top of mind.

“Clearly, we’re going to have to defend the president when the presumptive chairman says ‘lawyer up,’” Fallon told The Hill, referencing the two-word statement Garcia released the night of the midterms.

“That’s absolutely absurd and ridiculous, and it’s not fair-minded. We should go where the evidence leads us, not where politics drives us. And so, the president, the administration, his allies, major donors of conservative causes and candidates are going to need protection because I think that there’s going to be weaponization from the Democratic side. They’re going to have lawfare on steroids,” he added.

“We’re all looking for our best and highest use, and I want to take the years of experience that I’ve had as an entrepreneur, and hell, I’ve been on city council, state rep, state Senate, and now in Congress for six years.”

Fallon will face Gill, at 32 the youngest member of the House Republican conference this Congress.

Gill has made a name for himself on several fronts as a freshman lawmaker, both as a powerful fundraiser and for vocally taking on Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) as she pushed for passage of her immigration reform bill.

Gill said he sees the role as playing a part in getting Republicans back into the majority and even keeping a GOP leader in the White House.

“What you’re already seeing right now from Democrats who are coming in is a level of pettiness and animosity towards not just the president and his administration” but the broader government, he told The Hill.

“Our goal as Republicans in the minority on that committee is going to be to make sure that the rule of law is followed, that we are not allowing Democrats to weaponize that committee against the American people, which they’ve already signaled they’re willing to do, and to stand in the gap and to defend the rule of law.”

He also said while newer to Congress, he wasn’t concerned his youth would hamper his chances, taking a swipe at Democrats as they mull whether Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), the longtime top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, should continue to lead the panel.

“I would just say that the Republican Party is the party of meritocracy. The Democrat Party is the party of DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion] and judging Americans by their immutable characteristics. What differentiates us is that we are not elevating an 88-year-old with no knowledge of financial policy to be the chairman of the Financial Services Committee, for instance, we are looking at the best people we can possibly get to lead committees,” he said.

“And we do truly believe in a merit-based system, and I think that is a huge advantage of this party and this movement. And it’s a righteous difference.”
