articles.title: The Memo: Embattled Trump seeks reset with White House news conference
articles.summary: President Trump will seek a reset of sorts when he holds a press conference at the White House at noon EST Friday. Trump will appear in front of the media after being weakened by the major beating the GOP took in the midterm elections; while the war on Iran stands unresolved; and as he and…
articles.body:
President Trump will seek a reset of sorts when he holds a press conference at the White House at noon EST Friday.

Trump will appear in front of the media after being weakened by the major beating the GOP took in the midterm elections; while the war on Iran stands unresolved; and as he and his allies face uncertainty — and a spate of Democratic-led investigations — during the remaining two years of his presidency.

Even someone with Trump’s ability to shape the media narrative will struggle to turn the page on all those things. But he seems sure to try.

Trump announced the event via a social media post Thursday as he returned from what he termed a “Highly Consequential Trip” to Asia.

He framed the news conference as an opportunity to talk about trade deals with nations in the region. But virtually nobody expects those agreements to be the main focus.

“I imagine it will be more of the same from him [on trade]. That they had a wonderful meeting and reached a bunch of deals that he will have little to no details on,” Stephanie Grisham, who served as White House press secretary and communications director for about nine months of Trump’s first term, told this column.

Grisham, who is now often critical of the president, predicted that Trump would also play down the recent cascade of tech outages that have caused public disquiet and that he might “blame the midterms on cheating and the Iran war that people ‘just won’t understand had to happen.’”

Trump surprised some observers by accepting the outcome of the midterms at first, even as Democrats easily took the majority in the House and flipped nine Senate seats for a 56-44 majority. The Senate gain, finalized this week with a Democratic victory in a close race in Alaska, was the largest since 1958 .

The president fired off a social media post on Nov. 9 questioning whether anyone could “really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” however. That message received conspicuously little traction. The response from conservative commentator Megyn Kelly — “Just stop” — was indicative of widespread reluctance to take such claims seriously.

The Friday press conference will, at a minimum, allow Trump to create headlines and, perhaps, to sketch a path forward on some of the issues that loom large in the public mind. As ever, it is also possible the biggest news could come from some entirely unexpected direction.

The GOP’s defeat at the polls was largely driven by Trump’s low popularity ratings, which are in turn a consequence of the unpopular war and a perceived failure to address the cost of living. The two topics are linked given that gas prices, though lower than their peak, remain elevated from prewar levels.

There is speculation about what comes next in Iran, thanks in part to the president’s mixed signals.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he wrote on social media last week, seeming to suggest that he saw continuing economic pressure on the Islamic Republic as the best way to try to extract further concessions from Tehran. But another American aircraft carrier, the USS Roosevelt, arrived in the Middle East this week, keeping military options open.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Trump was mulling “extensive” new strikes on Iran, in part because he was “considering warnings from Israel about Iran’s success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals.”

Such an escalation would be highly contentious at home, though Trump may believe it could help deliver the kind of victory that has eluded him so far.

The president’s lagging poll numbers are also widely viewed as a sign of public weariness with his penchant for self-aggrandizement and chaos — including his controversial plans for the renovation of existing Washington landmarks and the construction of new ones in his honor.

Trump has given some characteristically mixed signals as to where he intends to go from here in the remaining two years of his presidency.

In an interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” right after the midterms, he admitted that his immigration enforcement actions have come to be seen as “too tough” by some people. Yet he also announced the promotion of Stephen Miller, perhaps the most hard-line member of the administration on immigration matters, to replace the departing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

“Trump has indicated through [elevating] Stephen Miller that he is ready to fight,” GOP strategist Ron Bonjean said. “At the same time, he has been complimentary of Democrats and deferential to them winning power. I think he is going to engage — or there is going to be one heck of a fight coming.”

To be sure, Trump has some political strengths on which he can draw. Even if more Republicans are now privately willing to express misgivings with his leadership in the wake of the midterms, few are inclined to do so publicly — a reminder of the firm grip he continues to exert on his party.

Even amid his low poll ratings, he retains the avid support of the roughly one-third of Americans who are firmly in the MAGA camp.

In terms of tactics, Trump seems likely to try to defy efforts by the new Democratic majorities to pump the brakes on his agenda. Many of his most sweeping actions have come by the use of executive power rather than through the legislative process, and that is likely to continue.

Allies in the White House — and further afield — are set to do their utmost to frustrate Democratic investigations, too.

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, on Monday wrote to incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) warning him to preserve documents. Reitz also asserted that “a committee’s gavel is not a prosecutor’s commission.”

There’s one more element of Friday’s news conference that will be closely watched: whether Trump tips his hand in terms of whom he currently favors to succeed him.

The ebbs and flows in the perceived fortunes of Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in particular, have become something of a Beltway obsession in this regard.

The 2028 speculation is a reminder that the post-Trump era is not so far away. But on Friday, it’s only Trump who will be center stage.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Thune fears GOP revolt over Medicaid cuts in Pentagon funding push
articles.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is leery about advancing a budget reconciliation package to fund the Pentagon as he and other GOP senators fear there will be a revolt within their ranks over reforms projected to reduce Medicaid spending by as much as $1 trillion. Thune has touted the changes to Medicaid that Republicans…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is leery about advancing a budget reconciliation package to fund the Pentagon as he and other GOP senators fear there will be a revolt within their ranks over reforms projected to reduce Medicaid spending by as much as $1 trillion.

Thune has touted the changes to Medicaid that Republicans enacted last year in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — also known as Working Families Tax Cut — as a big GOP accomplishment to rein in the growth of government.

But Thune is uncertain about whether he would be able to hold his conference together to fend off Democratic amendments to reverse Medicaid spending cuts if Republicans bring a budget reconciliation package to the Senate floor in the lame-duck session. That bill would provide an additional $350 billion to the Pentagon, something that President Trump has demanded.

Thune and other Senate GOP leaders are worried that Democrats could persuade a few Republican colleagues to join them in instructing the Senate Finance Committee to review the Medicaid reforms, which would open the door to later reversing them on the Senate floor.

“It’s a real concern,” acknowledged Senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), who would be tasked with managing a budget resolution and follow-up budget reconciliation package.

“We think we have colleagues in our midst who would try to overturn some of that stuff,” Johnson said of the reductions in Medicaid spending that Republicans used last year to offset the cost of tax cuts.

Johnson called the Medicaid changes “modest reforms” that “bring the spending curve down a little bit.”

But some Republicans worry that rural hospitals in their home states will get walloped by changes in the law slated to take effect next year and in 2028.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) said he supports keeping in place new work requirements for Medicaid beneficiaries, but he opposed provisions to reduce health care provider taxes, which states rely on to fund their Medicaid costs, and he opposed reductions in state directed payments.

“I’m for the work requirements but I imagine Democrats would want to reverse the provider tax for rural hospitals — I want to reverse the provider tax for rural hospitals,” Hawley told The Hill.

The American Hospital Association has warned that limits on how much revenue states can collect through provider taxes could create unpredictability for state Medicaid programs.

Hawley also said he’s told the Senate GOP leadership that he would insist on a vote to defund Planned Parenthood if he agrees to vote to begin the budget reconciliation process.

Other Republicans who could vote to reverse Medicaid funding cuts include Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who is up for re-election in 2028; Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who just lost her re-election bid; and retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who warned his colleagues against steep Medicaid cuts last year.

Polling showed that six in 10 midterm election voters said they were “very concerned” about health care costs and 33 percent of voters cited cuts to programs such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) as a reason to vote against Republicans.

A KFF analysist of The Voter Poll by SSRS, which was conducted from Oct. 19 to Nov. 3, found that voters who were concerned about health care costs preferred Democratic candidates over Republicans by a 2-to-1 margin in key Senate battlegrounds such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.

Complicating the political calculus for Thune is that Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown, the Democrat who won the Ohio Senate race, is due to replace Republican Sen. John Husted (R-Ohio) by Dec. 15, which would shrink the Senate GOP majority to 52 votes right when a budget reconciliation package is likely to come to the floor.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) noted that some of the Medicaid cuts included in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act survived by only a single vote.

He warned they could be reversed after Democrats pick up a seat in the lame-duck session once Brown, the Democrat, gets sworn into office.

“I think everything is at risk just because there were a number of areas in which savings were made — remember we only won those by one vote in a lot of cases. We will be down one person by that time” a budget reconciliation package comes to the Senate floor in December, Rounds said.

“Even if everybody voted the same, we would lose those votes because we’re short one member by the 15 th of December. It’s just a matter of math,” he said.

Rounds said keeping the Medicaid and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) reforms in place are critical to protecting the landmark individual and business tax cuts that Trump signed into law.

“It’s a matter of maintaining the entire tax bill,” he said. “If you start chipping away at all the provisions of it, it makes other areas more difficult to continue on.

“No tax on Social Security benefits for a lot of people was really valuable. But there were offsets. When it comes to ‘No Tax on Tips,’ there were offsets,” he added, arguing that popular tax breaks would be at risk if the offsets that were used to limit their impact on the federal deficit are erased.

Thune has warned his Republican colleagues that mustering 51 votes to begin debate on a budget resolution is only part of the challenge of using the budget reconciliation package to circumvent a Democratic filibuster.

He has repeatedly cautioned them that they would need to repeatedly muster a majority to fend off Democratic attempts to unwind core elements of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump’s signature legislative accomplishment.

“We’re talking to all of our members and getting an assessment of where folks ultimately will come down,” Thune said of his efforts to feel out how GOP senators would vote on a budget reconciliation package.

“It’s a function not just of being able to get on the bill, it’s also being able to protect it and defend once it’s on the floor,” he said. “That’s a different question for our members than whether you can get on the bill.”

He said that fighting off Democratic amendments to reverse Medicaid spending reductions and other reforms and other poison bills “is probably the most challenging part.”

articles.title: Rubio gains buzz while Vance’s fortunes falter in GOP race
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio is up and Vice President Vance is down when it comes to talk about the GOP presidential race. Rubio is generating growing buzz among Republicans as a potential 2028 presidential contender as the party looks for a savior in the aftermath of a midterm blitz by Democrats, who won 56 seats in…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is up and Vice President Vance is down when it comes to talk about the GOP presidential race.

Rubio is generating growing buzz among Republicans as a potential 2028 presidential contender as the party looks for a savior in the aftermath of a midterm blitz by Democrats, who won 56 seats in the Senate and at least 257 House seats.

The shellacking was widely seen as a repudiation of President Trump and has Republicans wondering if anyone closely aligned with the president, including Rubio, can win a race in 2028 against an ascendant Democratic Party.

Vance blamed the Iran war on the GOP losses a day after the elections, which led to criticism of the vice president in some GOP circles. It may also have made Trump unhappy. The president initially brushed off Vance’s remarks, but he’s also pointedly said the vice president should have said it was the right decision to go to Iran for U.S. security.

Now people close to Vance are sending the signal that he may not run at all for the presidency in 2028. There are also serious questions about whether Rubio will actually run, even as there appear to be growing calls to draft him into the race.

The reason is simple: Rubio is increasingly viewed as someone who could appeal to the party’s base while also attracting a wider coalition, having cultivated a political identity of his own even while serving in one of the Trump administration’s most prominent roles.

Rubio was a rising GOP star in the Tea Party era before becoming a Republican senator from Florida. He ran for president himself in 2016, memorably clashing with Trump on the debate stage.

But even as his standing in the party gains steam, questions are coming up about whether Rubio actually wants to mount another presidential campaign, particularly in an election that some in the GOP see as a difficult cycle for their party.

Some Rubio allies say a White House bid could carry more political risks than rewards, as Republicans grapple with their midterm losses and the future direction of a party that has been dominated by Trump for a decade.

Where MAGA goes after Trump on foreign policy, trade and a host of other issues is very much in play.

Rubio allies suggest it may benefit the Floridian to sit out the 2028 contest, spend time in the private sector and reemerge in 2032 as a presidential candidate.

His political calculations are also complicated by the president himself, who is expected to loom large over the race to succeed him. The fear for Rubio and other would-be contenders is that they wouldn’t be given enough breathing room to maneuver away from Trump’s positions and rhetoric.

It’s a problem Vance is already experiencing with the Iran war. He was seen as the conflict’s biggest internal critic, but his postelection criticism of the war was not well received in some GOP circles.

Rubio has walked the tightrope with Trump successfully, but it would be a narrow rope indeed as a GOP presidential candidate.

“There are a lot of unknowns, that’s the biggest problem,” said one Rubio ally, who also noted that the secretary of State has yet to sit down with his tight-knit inner circle to discuss any future plans.

One reason for the uncertainty, according to one former Trump aide, is that the president has asked Rubio to remain in the administration longer. Starting a presidential campaign while serving as secretary of State and national security adviser is a difficult trick.

Still, the former aide argued that Rubio is in the strongest position among other would-be rivals to win the GOP’s presidential nomination, including Vance, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin.

“I think the midterms have changed everyone’s calculus, and Rubio is best positioned to actually win in 2028, where Vance, Cruz and even DeSantis, who I think is the best conservative governor in the past 50 years, would all get smoked,” the former Trump aide said.

The former aide opined that Rubio would perform better in a presidential race in 2028 than someone outside the administration because he is a part of Trump World and would be better positioned to bring the party together.

“Because at the end of the day, the party will need to unify to have any chance at winning,” the aide added. “Rubio having that connective tissue with the president, but also the credibility for the folks who are desperate to move on puts him in the best actual position to see that unification happen. Right now there are 10 different factions, [and] Rubio is the best bridge for them all.”

Jason Cabel Roe, who served as a national spokesperson for Rubio’s 2016 presidential campaign, also said Rubio could fare the best among Republicans.

“I don’t think there’s any disputing that there is a very wide lane for him,” Cabel Roe said. “I think he’s demonstrated his skill set as Secretary of State, and … I think executed that as well as any member of the Trump Cabinet, without seeming to own a lot of the Trump liabilities.”

At the same time, some longtime Rubio allies acknowledge it will be an uphill climb for any Republican — much less a Republican who worked in the Trump administration — to win in 2028.

“On some level, I’m sure he wants to run, but I know there would have to be an obvious path if he were to get in,” one Rubio ally said. “And I’m not sure there is one.”

Though the midterms were a rebuke of Trump, Republicans expect the president will keep his grip on the party as they select his successor.

Trump has floated both Vance and Rubio as potential presidential candidates and even suggested a joint Vance-Rubio ticket .

“Regardless of how the midterms turned out, Trump has great influence over who the next Republican presidential nominee is going to be,” said Republican strategist Ford O’Connell, who served as a Trump surrogate.

Rubio allies say it makes sense that the secretary of State be a major part of the 2028 discussion.

New Hampshire Republican strategist Jim Merrill, who was the senior adviser for Rubio’s presidential campaign in the state, said while he expects a “robust” GOP field, “I think Secretary Rubio deserves every consideration.”

“I’m not surprised that people are taking a long look at him right now,” he added. “Timing is a very tricky thing in politics.”

“Whether he runs or not, I think his voice is going to be incredibly important. You know, not only to the Republican Party but to the country,” Merrill said.

articles.title: ‘I agree with the president’: incoming senator Abdul El-Sayed seeks to help Trump end military aid to Israel
articles.summary: Michigan senator-elect also secured a meeting with JD Vance, who called him a ‘terrible evil’ in lead-up to election
articles.body:
The incoming US senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said that he and Donald Trump are in agreement about ending foreign military aid to Israel – and he hopes to find more common ground with the US president when he takes office.

"I agree with the president – I can't believe I'm saying that – that we need to end foreign military aid that is unconditional to Israel, as well as Egypt and Saudi Arabia and Pakistan," the senator-elect said.

In a surprise election day announcement , Trump told Fox News that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year under an agreement reached with that country's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

"I think we need to be applying very basic international law to what Israel is and has been doing," El-Sayed added. "We should not continue to be running cover for them at the UN, at the ICC, at the ICJ."

He said he wants to see Congress change its posture on the US's relationship with Israel, starting by making sure the Democratic caucus is no longer funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby that spent heavily against El-Sayed in his election. The comments come after El-Sayed said he has secured a meeting with JD Vance. The senator would not share the agenda of the meeting, but confirmed that the vice-president's chief of staff reached out to him after his election victory.

El-Sayed has goaded the Trump administration into working with him. In recent days, he created a shiny gold "TrumpCare" card and said that Trump can call Medicare for All "TrumpCare" if it will help expand healthcare to more Americans.

Vance regularly attacked El-Sayed on the campaign trail, calling the incoming senator "terrible evil" and "corrupted".

After El-Sayed won his race, he called Vance "habibi", a term of endearment in Arabic, and joked about how the vice-president will have to preside over his swearing-in ceremony in January.

During an interview earlier this week on Fox, Vance said that if El-Sayed wants to work with the Trump administration "to make people's lives better", then he would find "very much a willing partner".

El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim US senator in January, overcame tens of millions of dollars spent against him, first in a closely watched primary and then a swing-state general election.

He has three immediate goals once he's sworn in, he told the Guardian: stopping the "nuclear bomb" of Medicaid cuts, ending the war in Iran and addressing the "stupid approach" to tariffs. He also plans to propose Medicare for All legislation, get to work on a voting rights legislation after the US supreme court gutted the Voting Rights Act, advance the Pro Act to expand union rights and overturn Citizens United, the supreme court decision that unleashed unfettered outside spending on campaigns.

El-Sayed is supporting the Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen's bid for the Senate leadership role. El-Sayed said Van Hollen, an advocate for Palestinian rights, would be an "amazing leader, and he's a departure from a lot of the instincts of the past". Van Hollen was an early supporter of El-Sayed in his primary election against the US representative Haley Stevens and campaigned for El-Sayed.

As part of his campaign promise to change the Washington establishment, El-Sayed said he won't be moving his family to the US capital, and will be spending a lot of time back in Michigan doing town halls and talking to voters.

El-Sayed has two young daughters. He's one of a large group of incoming senators and representatives who skewed younger this cycle and also have young children. The "somewhat erratic" schedule of the job makes it harder on people with kids, he said, so making the US Capitol building a "free and open place" for children would help. The Capitol should help "good senators and congresspeople also be good parents", he said.

"I think one of the challenges with service is that we forget that every public servant is a private servant too, and that's to their families, in particular to their children," El-Sayed said. "And those two things shouldn't be mutually exclusive."

Throughout his campaign, El-Sayed faced Islamophobic rhetoric, including from Trump and Republican officials. Though his campaign wasn't about defending himself, Michiganders rejected those attacks when they voted him in, and that was important, he said.

"There are a lot of kids who are watching," he said. "And when the president of the United States is attacking somebody for their name or how they pray, it's important that the people of the state of Michigan stood up and said, 'No, this is not how we want to be.' And I think they sent a message that was loud and clear, and I'm really grateful for that."

articles.title: Elon Musk's space giant cozies up to Dem power brokers as party vows to put his empire under siege
articles.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX hired five Democratic lobbyists as Democrats promise probes into Ukraine satellite claims, Pentagon reliance and Chinese investors.
articles.body: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has hired a team of veteran Washington lobbyists with Democratic connections as the party prepares to take control of Congress and intensify scrutiny of his business empire. Democratic lawmakers have signaled plans to investigate several aspects of Musk’s business dealings and government relationships, including allegations that SpaceX improperly restricted Ukraine’s satellite communications, whether the Pentagon has become overly dependent on the company and potential conflicts of interest stemming from Musk’s relationship with the Trump administration. Against that backdrop, newly released public records show SpaceX has retained five veteran lobbyists from Mehlman Consulting, a bipartisan D.C.-based government affairs firm, several of whom have deep ties to Democratic lawmakers and former administrations. SpaceX, with a market capitalization of nearly $2 trillion, is home to Musk's holdings in aerospace engineering, artificial intelligence, telecommunications and space transportation. If Democrats successfully knock it down a peg, the resulting loss in value could send shock waves throughout the economy. DEMOCRATS SET SIGHTS ON ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER MIDTERM WINS, BUT PRITZKER DRAWS A SURPRISING LINE Musk has worked to publicly distance himself from the right wing since the GOP's poor midterm performance, recently stating that he’s "not MAGA" at a New York Times summit. "I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much. Or maybe it would have been much worse without that," he said at the event. "I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that." HOW ELON MUSK GOT BACK IN TRUMP'S ORBIT AFTER NUCLEAR FALLOUT, INSIDERS REVEAL: 'WATER UNDER THE BRIDGE' Musk isn’t the first tech leader to throw money to Democratic operatives, seemingly to prepare for the incoming congressional majority. Palantir, another frequent target of Democratic criticism, has also retained lobbyists with ties to the party. "I think at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money, and they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability," Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former Biden administration official, told NPR of Palantir’s hirings. WHY CORPORATE AMERICA NEEDS ONE PLAYBOOK FOR A DIVIDED WASHINGTON AFTER NOVEMBER Technology stocks took a sharp hit in the days after Democrats won their stunning midterm victory, with AI infrastructure and data-center companies among the hardest hit as investors weighed the prospect of tighter regulation. The throng of lobbyists adds to Musk’s already large arsenal of paid influencers, which includes Republicans and Democrats at the state and federal levels. Musk’s new agents include the former deputy chief of staff to Sen. Maria Cantwell, who is slated to take over the powerful Commerce Committee in January, a former aide to Vice President Al Gore and a host of other one-time high-ranking Democratic staffers. The effective date of registration listed on the lobbying records was Oct. 1, around the time many were predicting Democrats would win control of Congress. articles.title: Lo que no se vio al acabar el debate de Sánchez y Feijóo: cómo reaccionaron ambos dirigentes, qué es lo que hicieron, con quiénes hablaron...
articles.standfirst: Dos formas distintas de gestionarlo por parte de Pedro Sánchez y de Alberto Núñez-Feijóo
articles.summary: Dos formas distintas de gestionarlo por parte de Pedro Sánchez y de Alberto Núñez-Feijóo
articles.body: El debate echó el cierre, el cronómetro se puso a cero y las cámaras siguieron captando detalles. Uno de ellos se ha convertido en protagonista en redes sociales: la distinta forma en la que dejaron el plató tanto Pedro Sánchez como Alberto Núñez Feijóo una vez finalizado el cara a cara. Por partes. Feijóo permanecía junto a la mesa del debate, varios miembros de su equipo se acercaron de inmediato para arroparlo. La primera fue María del Mar Sánchez Sierra, responsable de su estrategia de imagen y comunicación, que lo recibió con un abrazo. Al poco se sumaron otras figuras clave del entorno del líder del PP, entre ellas Borja Sémper, Marta Varela, Luis de la Matta y Lucas Martinón. Por su parte, Pedro Sánchez abandonó la tarima sin formar parte de ese corrillo. El presidente del Gobierno intercambió unas breves palabras con una persona de su equipo y después se dirigió hacia María Casado, moderadora del encuentro. La secuencia, captada por las cámaras, no tardó en viralizarse. Porque en un debate político no solo cuentan los argumentos. También los gestos. Y la imagen final dejó una fotografía llamativa: Feijóo rodeado por sus colaboradores mientras Sánchez se alejaba de la mesa en solitario. Durante el cara a cara, el líder socialista optó por un tono más contenido, centrado en defender la gestión de su Gobierno y rebatir las críticas de su rival. Incluso llegó a coincidir con Feijóo en algunos momentos. "Estoy medio de acuerdo con usted", reconoció en uno de los intercambios. Ya en el minuto de oro, Sánchez pidió a los ciudadanos acudir a las urnas el próximo 29 de noviembre y votar "con el alma". Mientras que Feijóo había optado desde su primera intención en un discurso más directo y señalando a su opositor en cada uno de los temas que iban saliendo.

articles.title: What does screentime really mean, and what’s a parent to do about it?
articles.summary: Here’s my best advice from all the data I have seen.
articles.body:
We have decided to raise our infant son with no screentime. I was adamant about it from way before he was born.

As someone with two older children, I certainly understand the appeal, ease and seductiveness of sticking a child in front of a screen while you get that much-needed five minutes. But as we all know, it has gone too far. I was at a “mommy and me” class recently and saw a mom holding her phone up to her child for an entire hour. It made me sad, sick and depressed all at the same time, for both of them.

But when the baby and I got home, I handed him off to my husband sitting in his easy chair, leaving them both to watching basketball. And I thought to myself: Wait, what have I just done? What exactly is a screen?

Most parents will say that a screen is the phone or iPad, but researchers mean every screen — the television in the den, the laptop for homework, the console at school, everything. And when you add it all together, the number for screentime is alarming — but the conclusions also get murky.

Children under eight years old spend an average of 2.5 hours on screens each day. That number hasn’t changed in the last six years. The difference? The device. Over 50 percent of children under eight now have their own device — a number that is way, way up. And the device has moved from the living room to the bedroom. By age two, four in 10 children have their own tablet. By age eight, one in four have their own cellphone. So the biggest question I had was whether watching television is the same as using a tablet.

The answer: It’s complicated. There are two differentiators.

The first is active versus passive viewing. Researchers separate passive watching, where the child just takes in content, from active viewing where the child interacts with a screen. A kid zoned out on cartoons is very different from a kid sounding out words with a parent beside him.

Second, the type of passive viewing — a child watching two-minute YouTube videos is in a very different position from a kid watching the Jetsons or basketball with his dad. That doesn’t change the total hours of screentime, but it has a very different result. Simply put, not all screentime is created equal.

The biggest cost of all this screentime is bedtime. More than half of children are watching screens right up until bed, against the recommendation that children need at least an hour gap between screens and sleep. It is the most damaging and the most difficult change to document.

So here’s my best advice from all the data I have seen: Pick a time that the screens go dark every night, not just for the kids but for everyone in the household. Keep all devices in the kitchen, not the bedrooms.

Just saying “no screen time” isn’t going to work and isn’t sustainable. But what you can control is when and what kind. Find old cartoons and make sure they are the original — think “Scooby Doo” or “The Jetsons” instead of the new addicting-attention deceiving versions. Have them watch old Nick-at-Nite shows like “Bewitched,” “Happy Days,” or “I Love Lucy.” Have them watch sports.

Stop the screens from being small and in the bedrooms and go back to family TV-watching. Screens can actually be good family bonding time. And never, ever allow screens at meal times. Some people argue that no screen is morally superior to other screens. But research and common sense show that they are wrong.

This all goes for parents too. While I was writing this article, I looked at my own screentime. It made me feel sick, especially when I added up how much time over the course of my life I am spending and wasting on my screen. I don’t think I’m alone in that.

Dr. Liberty Vittert Capito is a professor of the practice of data science at the Olin Business School at Washington University in St. Louis. She is co-host of the Harvard Data Science Review podcast and the MIT data science podcast.

articles.title: Van Hollen scores support from another Dem amid Senate majority leader bid
articles.summary: Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she will back Sen. Chris Van Hollen for the Senate Democratic leadership role as he challenges Sen. Chuck Schumer.
articles.body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said Thursday she will back Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., as he challenges current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for the majority leader slot. Van Hollen announced a bid for the role last week. "I've been clear as well that I don't think that Senator Schumer is best positioned to be our next leader. I'm encouraged that people like Chris Van Hollen got in the race, and because I've been clear that I wasn't supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen," Slotkin stated in a video posted to social media. Van Hollen shared Slotkin's post on X and wrote, "@SenatorSlotkin & I agree: the American people spoke, and we need new leadership in the United States Senate. Now is the time to act boldly, and we’re going to work together to deliver results." TOP DEM CRIES 'WEAPONIZATION' AS COMMENTS WARNING YOUNG PEOPLE NOT TO JOIN TRUMP ADMIN LAND HER IN HOT WATER Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed — who will become the junior senator from Michigan early next year and is backing Van Hollen for the majority leader role — also shared Slotkin's post. "Michigan for @ChrisVanHollen," El-Sayed wrote. His post included a raised fist emoji. Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, who is also supporting Van Hollen's leadership bid, shared Slotkin's post and added, "Americans spoke. Democrats are listening." articles.title: GOP battles itself over defense funding
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Reconciliation push faces obstacles ▪ Trump to give presser on Asia trip ▪ Senate passes permitting reform bill ▪ U.N. court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide Republicans in Washington are struggling to find a path forward on the Pentagon’s $350 billion reconciliation ask, as President Trump pushes lawmakers to approve more funding…
articles.body:
▪ U.N. court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide

Republicans in Washington are struggling to find a path forward on the Pentagon’s $350 billion reconciliation ask, as President Trump pushes lawmakers to approve more funding before Democrats take control in January.

After multiple conference meetings this week to discuss the administration’s request for a party-line push, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) signaled he would first try a different approach.

“We want to explore all the possibilities for funding the military, one of which would be seeing whether or not there’s an appetite on the Democrat side to do it,” Thune said Wednesday after meeting with his conference.

“I don’t know that they will. But we think that we ought to at least explore that possibility ,” he added.

Senate Republicans have warned that the president’s push for GOP leaders to rely on budget reconciliation — which would bypass the need for Democratic input — could risk a government shutdown, as the Dec. 11 deadline to keep the government funded fast approaches.

It could also derail progress on the nearly $1.1 trillion defense appropriations bill for fiscal 2027 and accompanying National Defense Authorization Act. House Armed Services Chair Mike Rogers (R-Ala.) said Thursday that the must-pass defense bill could be ready for a vote after Thanksgiving.

Some Senate Democrats have signaled that they are looking to use that looming Dec. 11 government funding deadline to force the White House to end the war with Iran, which has lasted more than eight months.

Sens. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) announced on Thursday that they will move to add an amendment to appropriations bills to block funding for offensive operations against Iran.

So far, the Pentagon has shown no signs of backing off its call on Capitol Hill to push through the $350 billion party-line package, which would include funding to expand weapons production and replenish stockpiles used in the Iran war, along with funding for minerals, artificial intelligence and the president’s Golden Dome missile defense initiative.

Pentagon Deputy Secretary Steve Feinberg joined the Senate GOP l unch on Wednesday to discuss the package, The Hill’s Filip Timotija and Helen Huiskes reported. Republicans were still split after the meeting.

Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) told reporters afterward that reconciliation will “probably not” happen this week, but added, “ We are not taking it off the table at all.”

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said he supports the $350 billion package, noting that discussions were ongoing, while Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) nodded to the midterm losses while discussing his opposition to the proposal.

“I’m not for a partisan Republican bill to spend more money or borrow more money,” Paul said, The Washington Post reported. “There’s quite a few of them that I guess did not, were not aware of what happened with the election recently. All the exit polling showed that people were upset about the price of gas and the Iran war.”

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), meanwhile, left the meeting describing the internal debate as a “jump ball.”

“Everybody recognizes it’s going to be a herculean effort to get the House and the Senate in terms of the scope and the process,” Cornyn told reporters after leaving the meeting.

Over on the House side, the prospects of getting $350 billion across the finish line are not looking much better. Rogers signaled there could be a path forward on a smaller package.

“By the way, 350 is not going to happen. You may have guessed that, but a reconciliation bill is still possible. It’s going to have to be skinny down to deal with first and foremost the hole in the defense budget that Venezuela and Iran have created,” Rogers said during a Hudson Institute event this week.

The Iran war also appears to be causing growing turmoil in the White House. The New York Times reported Trump has grown frustrated with Vice President Vance for his post-midterm assessment that the Iran war was to blame for GOP losses.

Senate Republicans were largely united in blocking a war powers measure yesterday that would have directed the president to end hostilities in Iran. The White House has noted, however, that, even if it passed as a concurrent resolution, the measure would mostly be symbolic and not be enforceable.

The vote failed 48-51. Republican Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Paul, who have all voted for similar Iran war powers resolutions in the past, joined all Democrats except Sen. John Fetterman (Pa.) in backing the measure.

“I’ve supported some. I mean, you do know resolutions differ from each one. This one doesn’t go to the president, so it’s just a statement from Congress,” S en. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said, nodding to his past support for other versions of the resolution. “I’ve made that statement. I don’t need to vote on a Democrat resolution to make that statement.”

▪ The Hill : Exiting GOP senators become liability for Trump.

▪ The Hill Insider : House Republicans race for key roles in fight over Trump probes.

Republicans have less than a month of legislating time left in Washington, D.C. before the Democratic-controlled Congress takes over in January. Rep. Ryan Zinke (R-Mont.) is one of the many Republicans on his way out, as he chose not to seek reelection. Part of the report card for Republicans over the past two years includes continuing to rack up multi-trillion-dollar deficits. I asked Zinke if he viewed that as a failure.

“I would describe it as punting. Every time a tough issue comes out, what does Congress do? Punts,” Zinke said . “We’ve been punting for a long time.”

The Democratic record is the same, a roughly equal contributor over time to the current $40 trillion national debt. That’s a longer-term issue that likely isn’t going to be solved anytime soon. For now, both sides need to come together before December to simply make sure the government doesn’t shut down over the holidays.

The Department of Justice has filed to dismiss its lawsuit seeking to block the certification of Alaska’s Senate race if Mary Peltola (D) won, following projections of her victory. The DOJ argued a third candidate named Dan J. Sullivan could confuse voters and cost Sen. REPORTING BACK : Trump is set to hold a press conference today at noon following his return from a multiday trip to Asia to tout achievements from the two summits he attended.

He called the trip to China, in which he met with both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin , “great and highly consequential” in a Truth Social post Thursday announcing the presser at the White House. He said he would also discuss trade deals that were made with Thailand, the Philippines and others during his stop in the Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations conference.

The most high-profile part of the entire trip was the unprecedented trilateral meeting Trump had with Xi and Putin. The leaders agreed to a four-point “peace declaration” to engage in ongoing dialogue on nuclear nonproliferation.

Trump’s kind words for both dictators also stirred an uneasy reaction from critics who have denounced his warm relations with America’s most powerful rivals.

Trump did not hold a press conference in Asia before leaving, which presidents typically do at the end of high-profile visits abroad. Media coverage of the visit was also tightly controlled.

TIME PERMITTING : The Senate has approved a key permitting reform bill to speed up the buildout of the country’s energy and infrastructure projects, but now the test will be if the legislation has the time and support to get through the House .

The upper chamber passed the bill by a vote of 62-33 on Thursday, with backing from most Republicans and some Democrats. The bill seeks to address complaints from various industries that building in the U.S. takes too long, while opponents argue it would be bad for the environment through loosening environmental laws and bolstering fossil fuels and mining.

The bill is expected to have bipartisan support in the House, though Democrats are split on the provisions. And the main hurdle could be the limited time left before the end of the term with an already crowded lame-duck calendar.

CLIMATE COUNTDOWN: Today is the deadline for global leaders to reach a climate agreement at the COP31 summit in Turkey, as disagreements over fossil fuels and funding for developing nations threaten to send the negotiations into overtime.

The United Nations climate summit, slated to take place Nov. 9 to 20, brought together negotiators from nearly 200 countries to work on the agreement. But a revised draft released Thursday dropped explicit references to fossil fuels, drawing backlash from climate activists and from countries pushing for stronger commitments to transition away from coal, oil and gas. The draft also removed a proposed $120 billion annual target for funding to help developing countries adapt to climate change.

Countries must reach a consensus to adopt a final agreement, but negotiations have frequently run past their scheduled end dates and could continue into the weekend if the countries fail to resolve their differences in time.

RECORD LAUNCH : The AI giant Anthropic went public on Thursday with a record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) that surpassed $80 billion.

The firm announced Wednesday that certain stockholders sold 980 million shares of the company’s stock valued at $83 per share. Anthropic then opened at $111.50 per share upon its opening on the stock market, trading under the ticker “ANT.”

The stock finished just above $97 per share at the end of the day. Elon Musk ‘s SpaceX previously held the record for an IPO, raising $75 billion as it went public at $150 per share in June.

The House will convene at 10:30 a.m. for a pro forma session.

Sen Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) speaks during an event at the renamed Donald J Trump Institute of Peace, Sept. 3, 2026, in Washington. (Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press)

CAPITOL CRYPTO FORUM : What will the incoming Congress mean for the cryptocurrency industry? That question dominated conversation with lawmakers and industry leaders at The Hill’s “Capitol Crypto Forum” on Thursday.

Members of both parties expressed some cautious optimism that a key bill setting a federal regulatory framework for the crypto industry could have a path forward in the next session of Congress.

Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), the chair of the House Financial Services Committee, pointed to the 78 House Democrats who supported the Clarity Act as evidence that the industry has support across the aisle.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said he had conversations with Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), a longtime crypto critic, in which she said she wants regulations in place.

“I’ll blow all your minds. I’ve had conversations with Elizabeth Warren, where she says, ‘I want the industry regulated. I just don’t want the industry to write the regulations,’” Moreno said.

The Clarity Act stalled in the Senate in September, leaving many wondering if Congress missed its best chance at passing the top item on crypto’s legislative agenda.

At the same time, crypto has found itself caught in the midst of a political crossfire as the industry spent millions to support crypto-friendly candidates in the midterms and was handed some major defeats . There’s also internal divisions within the Democratic Party on its stance, said Peter Van Valkenburgh , the executive director of Coin Center.

“There’s a very strong anti-tech vision being articulated in parts of the Democratic Party, and the voices for a tech-forward Democratic Party, they haven’t found their song yet,” he said.

LANDMARK RULING : The United Nations’s highest court has found that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim population, an ethnic minority in the southeast Asian country.

The decision marks the first time ever that the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has held a state responsible for committing genocide through violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention, which was adopted in the aftermath of the Holocaust.

The ICJ and other international courts have previously recognized that genocide took place in three countries — Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge in the 1970s, Rwanda in 1994 and Bosnia with respect to the Srebrenica killings in 1995. But this is the first time that a state itself has been declared responsible for a genocide.

The court stated that Myanmar’s military, police and border guards killed about 10,000 Rohingya civilians in incidents that included mass shootings, sexual violence and arson. The attacks led more than 810,000 civilians out of the Myanmar state of Rakhine to seek refuge in Bangladesh.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to immediately cease all ongoing violations, take steps to investigate those suspected of committing acts of genocide, ensure acts of genocide don’t continue and adopt measures to bring restitution to the Rohingya. It gave a two-year timeline for the country to report back on these efforts.

Gambia, a largely Muslim country in Africa, first filed the case against Myanmar seven years ago following the “clearance operations” there in 2017.

ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said nine judges on the court voted in favor of the ruling and six dissented.

Myanmar has been in the midst of a civil war between the military and pro-democracy resistance forces since 2021. The country has previously denied accusations of genocide.

articles.title: Washington state finds Nippon Dynawave knew conditions were unsafe ahead of tank implosion
articles.summary: Washington state fined Nippon Dynawave $10 million Friday, saying the company willfully disregarded health and safety violations ahead of a chemical tank burst that killed 11 workers and injured a dozen others. The Washington State Department of Labor & Industries (L&I) said Friday that the penalty is the largest health and safety fine in state…
articles.body:
Washington state fined Nippon Dynawave $10 million Friday, saying the company willfully disregarded health and safety violations ahead of a chemical tank burst that killed 11 workers and injured a dozen others.

The Washington State Department of Labor & Industries (L&I) said Friday that the penalty is the largest health and safety fine in state history.

“On May 26, 2026, the company’s inaction led to the worst industrial disaster in modern state history,” the department said in a release. “Dozens of violations related to that tank, other tanks on the site, the company’s emergency response, and the environmental impact have resulted in a combined $10,138,127 in penalties and cost recovery from state agencies.”

The Evergreen State said it would go a step further and refer Nippon to criminal authorities for investigation.

“Because Nippon’s safety and health violations were both willful and contributed directly to the deaths of their workers, L&I will also refer the case to the appropriate authorities for potential criminal prosecution,” the department said.

A representative for Nippon did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

A chemical tank holding white liquor, an ingredient for making paper, burst in May at Nippon’s paper mill in Longview, Wash., which the state called “the worst industrial disaster in modern state history.”

The state’s investigation, which interviewed more than 70 witnesses and reviewed tens of thousands of documents, found that the tank’s walls were thinner than the safe level and repair was mandated by state law. The department said that the Nippon received multiple reports of corroded walls that put the integrity of the tank at risk but did not act.

Joel Sacks, the director of the labor and industries department, called the state’s findings “shocking and heartbreaking” in a statement.

“Nippon Dynawave had all the information they needed to act, but they didn’t listen to alarms their consultants and staff were raising. Tragically, there are 11 families whose loved ones never came home as a result, and many others whose lives will be changed forever,” Sacks said.

After the disaster at Nippon and a near-disaster around the same time at a chemical plant in California, critics called for greater environmental regulation, especially at chemical sites.

President Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency had recently moved to roll back some regulations that impacted chemical plants, but the agency said the changes would not have impacted the incidents in Washington or California.

articles.body:
President Trump floated his newly appointed chief of staff, longtime adviser Stephen Miller, as a potential presidential candidate — asking the top White House official if he was interested in the presidency during a press conference Friday afternoon.

The comment came after Miller heaped praise on the president, with whom the chief of staff has worked since the start of Trump’s political career.

“No president has done what he has done over the last two years,” Miller said during the conference following the president’s visit to China earlier in the week, where he participated in rare trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“Under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history, and I’m so proud to be his chief of staff,” he added.

After Miller’s remarks, Trump joked with reporters in the briefing room, saying, “We have breaking news, he was better than these two guys,” referring to Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Both men spoke earlier in the conference

“Do you want to run for president?” Trump asked Miller.

Both Rubio and Vance have been floated among the GOP as possible presidential candidates for 2028, though neither has formally announced a bid. Vance told Fox News this week he would decide on running “sometime next year.”

Though Rubio has reportedly said he’s not planning on a run next cycle, speculation surrounding his potential candidacy has continued to rise as Republicans look toward 2028 following a poor midterm performance.

Vance and Rubio also lauded the president during the press conference, congratulating him on striking trade deals with the Philippines and Thailand during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila earlier in the week.

Vance commended Trump’s work to “reorganize the global economy so that it makes sense to invest in the United States of America.”

Rubio also celebrated the president’s trilateral talks with Russia and China, which were divisive on both sides of the political aisle, pointing out that the three countries — despite being adversaries — collectively possess “the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet.”

“I am glad these leaders were able to engage,” Rubio said. “It set the tone and created a platform — created a foundation upon which, hopefully, the hard work of diplomacy and trade negotiations can occur.”
